adjust.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is for senior drivers and the people who care about them. Senior driving demands physical, visual, and mental ability, and the day may come when it makes sense to limit driving, or to stop, either for a while or for good. We will look at the warning signs that a driver may be unsafe, the practical ways seniors can limit their driving to stay safe, and where to find a self-assessment questionnaire. The goal is not to take driving away, but to help drivers notice changes early and adjust in ways that keep them and others safe.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What driving demands","fact_ids":["sec13-F01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Physical, visual and mental ability.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01"]},{"text":"Limits or stopping may come.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Senior driving demands physical, visual, and mental ability. As those abilities change, the day may come to limit driving or to stop, temporarily or permanently. This is a matter of honest self-assessment rather than age alone. The handbook allows for both temporary and permanent changes. Recognizing that both limiting and stopping are options makes the decision less all-or-nothing. A driver who notices changes can often keep driving safely by making adjustments long before stopping becomes necessary. Driving takes physical, visual and mental ability.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":33,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Warning signs","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Getting lost in familiar places.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]},{"text":"Dents and scrapes.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]},{"text":"Frequent close calls or collisions.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"The handbook lists clear warning signs that a driver may be unsafe. The first is getting lost in familiar places. The second is new dents and scrapes on the car, or on other property. The third is frequent close calls or collisions. Any of these is a reason to pay attention. They do not automatically mean a person must stop driving, but they are signals that something has changed and that the driver should look at how, when, and where they drive, and consider the coping steps in the next part of this lesson. Frequent close calls are a warning sign.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Ways to adjust","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Curb night driving; use lit routes.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},{"text":"Light-traffic hours; skip freeways.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},{"text":"Shorter trips; a right-side mirror.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Senior drivers may adjust in several ways. They may cut back on night driving, using well-lit routes when they must drive at night. They may favor hours with light traffic, avoid difficult intersections, shorten trips to essentials, skip freeways, and add a right-side mirror. Each of these lowers the demands of driving. The Driver Skills Self-Assessment Questionnaire, on the DMV driver skills page, can help a driver decide which adjustments make sense. Together, warning signs and coping steps let a driver respond to change in measured ways.","fact_ids":["sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"All or nothing","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F03","sec13-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Trap: keep driving as usual or quit.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F03","sec13-F02"]},{"text":"Truth: limiting is an option first.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F03","sec13-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap. Families and drivers often frame the choice as keep driving exactly as before or give up the keys entirely. The handbook describes a middle path: the day may come to limit or stop driving, temporarily or permanently, and seniors may first curb night driving, favor light-traffic hours, avoid hard intersections, shorten trips, skip freeways, and add a right-side mirror. A second trap is ignoring the warning signs. Getting lost in familiar places, new dents and scrapes, and frequent close calls are signals to act, not to brush aside.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F03","sec13-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check your understanding","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Name a warning sign.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: name a warning sign that a driver may be unsafe. Decide on your answer. The handbook lists getting lost in familiar places, new dents and scrapes on the car or property, and frequent close calls or collisions. If you named any of these, you have the warning signs. When they appear, the next step is to look at ways to adjust, such as driving during light-traffic hours, skipping freeways, or shortening trips, and to take the Driver Skills Self-Assessment Questionnaire on the DMV driver skills page.","fact_ids":["sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Fitness recap","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Ability first; watch the signs.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},{"text":"Adjust before stopping.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"To wrap up, senior driving demands physical, visual, and mental ability, and the day may come to limit or stop driving, temporarily or permanently. Warning signs include getting lost in familiar places, dents and scrapes, and frequent close calls or collisions. Seniors may adjust by curbing night driving and using lit routes when needed, favoring light-traffic hours, avoiding hard intersections, shortening trips to essentials, skipping freeways, and adding a right-side mirror. The Driver Skills Self-Assessment Questionnaire on the DMV driver skills page can help guide those choices.","fact_ids":["sec13-F01","sec13-F02","sec13-F03","sec13-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec13-u02","module_id":"sec13-m02","objective_ids":["sec13-u02"],"title":{"text":"Renewal Liaison.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers license renewal for drivers seventy and older and the Community Liaison, a DMV resource for seniors, teens, and all Californians. Renewal at seventy or older follows its own steps, including an in-person visit and a vision test. The Community Liaison champions public safety and fair treatment and offers tools and information, but there are things it cannot do. We will look at the renewal steps, when notices arrive and what to do if one does not, and exactly what the liaison can and cannot help with.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Renewing at seventy or older","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Renew in person with a vision test.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"eLearning knowledge tests when required.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"Notices about ninety days out.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drivers who are seventy or older when their license expires must renew in person, with a vision test and possibly other exams. When a knowledge test is required, they are eligible to take it through eLearning. Renewal notices are mailed about ninety days before expiry. If a notice does not arrive, the driver can apply on the DMV license services page or at an office, and sample tests are available on the DMV driver education page. So seventy-plus renewal pairs an in-person vision test with eLearning options and notices about ninety days ahead.","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The Community Liaison","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Public safety for all Californians.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"Focus on seniors and teens.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"No hearing representation.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"The Community Liaison champions public safety for all Californians, with a focus on seniors and teens. It mediates to help make sure drivers are treated fairly, lawfully, and with dignity, and it offers many tools and much information. It is barred, however, from representing drivers at hearings and reexaminations. So the liaison is an advocate and a source of help, not a legal representative. Putting the unit together: senior fitness pairs ability demands with honest limits, renewal at seventy brings in-person vision testing, and the liaison pairs advocacy with a no-representation limit.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The liaison as lawyer","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"Trap: the liaison represents you.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},{"text":"Truth: it mediates but cannot represent.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap. Drivers facing a hearing or reexamination sometimes expect the Community Liaison to represent them. The liaison is barred from hearing and reexamination representation. It can mediate for fair, lawful, and dignified treatment and offer tools and information, but it does not stand in for the driver. A second trap is waiting indefinitely for a renewal notice. Notices are mailed about ninety days before expiry, and if one does not come, the driver can apply on the DMV license services page or at an office rather than letting the license lapse.","fact_ids":["sec13-F06","sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u02-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check your understanding","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]},"lines":[{"text":"When do renewal notices arrive?","fact_ids":["sec13-F05","sec13-R01"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: about how many days before expiry are renewal notices mailed? Drivers seventy or older at expiry renew in person with a vision test and possibly other exams, and may take required knowledge tests through eLearning. If you answered about ninety days, you have the notice rule. We will look at how to contact Community Liaison and Outreach, what progressive dementia means for driving and who can step in, the Mature Driver Improvement Program and the insurance discounts it can bring, and the no-fee ID cards available to seniors and to unsafe drivers of any age. Several numbers appear here, including ages, hours, and years, so we will keep each one tied to its program. These resources help seniors stay safe on the road and keep their independence after they stop driving.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Liaison contact and dementia","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"One Community Liaison phone line.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Dementia ultimately ends safe driving.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Others may need to step in.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Contact with area outreach and the Community Liaison runs through the Community Liaison and Outreach phone line. Progressive dementia ultimately ends safe driving. When that happens, caregivers, physicians, and law enforcement may need to stop the senior from driving and arrange other transportation. Details about reexamination are on the DMV reexamination page. So liaison contact centers on one phone line, and dementia pairs the eventual loss of safe driving with intervention by caregivers, physicians, and officers, who help the senior move to other ways of getting around.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The mature driver program","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Eight hours, drivers fifty-five plus.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Insurance discounts possible.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Certificate valid three years.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"The Mature Driver Improvement Program is an eight-hour course for drivers fifty-five and older, covering topics of special interest to mature drivers. Insurers may offer discounts to graduates who show their completion certificate. The certificate is valid for three years and can be renewed through four-hour refresher courses from DMV-approved providers, listed on the DMV seniors page. So the program pairs an eight-hour course for drivers fifty-five and older with insurer discounts, three-year certificates, and four-hour renewals. Each number belongs to a different part of the program.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"No-fee ID cards","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Senior ID: sixty-two and older.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Unsafe drivers of any age may swap.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"ID-only cards.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Drivers sixty-two and older qualify for no-fee Senior ID cards. Unsafe drivers of any age may trade their license for a no-fee ID card that is good for identification only. Details are on the DMV ID card page. So senior IDs pair no-fee eligibility at sixty-two and older with an any-age swap for unsafe drivers. Both options let a person who stops driving keep an official way to prove their identity at no cost. Note that the senior ID age of sixty-two is different from the mature driver program age of fifty-five. Unsafe drivers of any age may trade a license for an ID-only card.","fact_ids":["sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Mixing up the numbers","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Trap: one age, one length for everything.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Truth: fifty-five, sixty-two, eight, three, four.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap built from the numbers. The Mature Driver Improvement Program is for drivers fifty-five and older and lasts eight hours. The certificate is valid three years and renews with a four-hour refresher. No-fee Senior ID cards start at sixty-two. Mixing these up is easy, so tie each number to its place: fifty-five and eight to the course, three and four to the certificate and refresher, and sixty-two to the senior ID card. A second trap is assuming the certificate never expires; it lasts three years. The senior ID starts at sixty-two.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check your understanding","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"The mature driver program.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]},{"text":"How long is it?","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: how long does the Mature Driver Improvement Program last? Choose your answer. The answer is eight hours. The course is for drivers fifty-five and older and covers topics of special interest to mature drivers. Graduates may get insurance discounts, the certificate is valid three years, and it renews with a four-hour refresher course from a DMV-approved provider. If you answered eight hours, you have the course length. If you answered four, you used the refresher length, so keep eight for the course and four for the refresher.","fact_ids":["sec13-F09","sec13-R02","sec13-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec13-u03-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Section wrap-up","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Liaison line; dementia ends driving.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},{"text":"Course at fifty-five; free ID at sixty-two.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]}],"narration":{"text":"To finish this section, area outreach and liaison contact runs through the Community Liaison and Outreach phone line. Progressive dementia ultimately ends safe driving, and caregivers, physicians, and law enforcement may need to stop the senior from driving and arrange other transport. The Mature Driver Improvement Program is eight hours for drivers fifty-five and older, and insurers may discount graduates whose certificates last three years and renew with four-hour refreshers. Drivers sixty-two and older qualify for no-fee Senior ID cards, and unsafe drivers of any age may swap a license for a no-fee ID card.","fact_ids":["sec13-F07","sec13-F08","sec13-F09","sec13-F10","sec13-F11","sec13-R02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]}]}
